Endless Exile: Children with Immigrant Parents**

Sherry Huang

Sherry Huang

Email: sherry.huang@gmail.com

Sherry Huang   Grew up in the Long Island suburbs and graduated from Barnard College with a B.A. in English. For more than a decade she worked as an editor for online publications, then as a project manager, before shifting toward marketing and communications at a non-profit. With some encouragement from her analyst, she enrolled in the master's program at NYGSP to start her journey toward a degree in psychoanalysis.

Building on personal experience and theory, the author examines how children with immigrant parents experience exile from their cultural origins as they assimilate into American culture. A liminal space is navigated in search of selfhood and an evolving parent/child dynamic. The author explores, through an Asian American lens, how these children might be “parentified” to achieve the American Dream, which creates a perpetual sense of Otherness and loss that lasts into adulthood.

Exploring the ways in which gender presentation is used as a possible solution to pre-oedipal conflicts and severe trauma, the author takes a snapshot of the treatment, written in the form of a theatrical play. Through analysis of the patient's somatization, agoraphobia, and difficult enactments, the author becomes aware of the patient's early disturbances in attachment and separation from the primitive mother. Analyst and patient both engage in an unconscious mutual disavowal of the patient's penis. As the analyst allows herself to make the penis thinkable, so too does the patient. What results is the ability for the patient to talk about her penis, and the trauma it represents, opening up space for the patient's gender presentation to expand during the course of treatment.

Not with the Spirit but with the Body: Subjectivity in Mrs. Dalloway**

Nick Smart

Nick Smart

Email: Nickdavidsmart@gmail.com

Nick Smart   Student at CMPS. He holds a PhD in English and American Literature from New York University and is Professor Emeritus at The College of New Rochelle where he taught English and Women's Studies. He is the author of “On Not Knowing Virginia Woolf” in the MLA's Approaches to Teaching Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, and “The Last Bob Dylan Record” in Tearing the World Apart: Bob Dylan and the Twenty-First Century. His interests include psychosomatic illness and the mental health of adolescents.

Mrs. Dalloway, published in 1925, is received as a surpassing example of Virginia Woolf's ability to create fiction that models the workings of the mind, an effect often called stream of consciousness by literary critics. Considering Woolf's biography, the author suggests a link between mind and body in the presentation of character and how this deepens Woolf's association with psychoanalytic thought.

Freud introduced the cliché as a model to understand transference: a timeless repetition of unfulfilled wishes and scenarios that are enacted unconsciously to attempt a different resolution of a conflict. Based on observations from a clinical case, the author argues that analytic space shares qualities of timelessness, and thus, can be understood as a projective canvas onto which transference can crystalize. The author reviews the expressions of transference and countertransference experienced with a patient over the course of a year, highlighting the role of fantasy, enactments, and displacement in the dyad resulting in the author understanding transference as not that of a cliché, but as a fractal filled with repetitions, role reversals, and identifications.

Annika Boras

Annika Boras

16 West Tenth Street
New York, NY 10011

Annika Boras   Currently in her first year of the master's program at the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP). She is a graduate of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA), London.

The author investigates the impact of current popular culture trends, particularly social media and reality television, on the emergence and maintenance of primitive psychological states in individuals. Drawing on the writings of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Otto Kernberg, and others, the author argues that the psychological strategies and structures evoked by social media and reality television are akin to those found in borderline personality and narcissism. While these primitive states can be temporary, the author posits that the widespread presence of those states threatens psychological maturation and fosters a more regressive, divided, and superficial society.

Late in May 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a statement that, in the then-forthcoming eleventh edition of the International Classification of Diseases, the diagnostic categories of “transsexualism” and “gender identity disorder of children” would be replaced with “gender incongruence of adolescence and adulthood” and “gender incongruence of childhood,” respectively. Both moved out of the “Mental and behavioural disorders” chapter and into the new “Conditions related to sexual health” chapter, in order to reflect “current knowledge that trans-related and gender diverse identities are not conditions of mental ill-health, and that classifying them as such can cause enormous stigma” (WHO, 2023). This development signified an important shift towards the long awaited depathologization of trans identities/lived experiences with the endorsement of a global authority. Up until now though, the dominant view in psychiatry and psychoanalysis regarding queer and trans patients remains that of pathologizing hermeneutics.

The convergence of psychoanalysis with the U.S. medical system is marked by two main epochs relevant to this current review: the post-war period (1950 to late 1960s) when psychiatry dominated mental health treatment and the current post-pandemic period that has resulted in the expansion of virtual, Telehealth services alongside a medical insurance system that has aggressively limited the number of treatments allowed (as well as limits on the length of treatment).

Following World War II, newly arrived psychoanalytic clinicians and theoreticians arriving in the U.S. aspired to continue developing pre-war European psychoanalysis within a North American context. The influx of non-physician lay analysts were confronted by a uniquely American interpretation of Freudian psychoanalysis. Between 1950 and the late 1960s, psychiatry emerged as the medium for transmission and the unofficial regulatory body that determined how psychoanalysis should be taught and practiced.

Non-physician psychoanalysts, who had previously thrived in the pre-war “lay analysis” period outside of North America, were experiencing a compromising transition when emigrating into what might be described as the U.S. “neo-Freudian medical model of psychoanalysis.” Within this model, psychiatry ascended even more powerfully as the gatekeeper of psychoanalysis. 126

Mary Landers

Mary Landers

Mary Landers  

Leader's stated aim in writing Jouissance: Sexuality, Suffering and Satisfaction is to go beyond the term jouissance as a catch-all for any symptom, and to “encourage a questioning of the term.” Any reader looking for a single categorical definition of the term will be disappointed. Those looking for an in-depth discussion of drive theory will be quite satisfied. Although Leader addresses the reader as “we Lacanians,” one need not be initiated to derive a great deal about the symptoms of neurosis, the function and limitation of language and the mind's ability to trick itself. This is accomplished on the premise that the body is the force behind the drive and the mind is its functionary.

Remembering Theodore Laquercia

Dr. Theodore “Ted” Laquercia died peacefully on April 13, 2023 after battling long-term illnesses. A graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, he was a beloved teacher, supervisor, analyst, member of the president's council and board of trustees. He was also an integral part of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, holding many positions over the years—president, provost, faculty, and administrator—and always helping students to flourish. He will be greatly missed as we remember him with appreciation and take inspiration from his dedication to all aspects of his work.

Lindsey Randol PsychD LPC-S

Lindsey Randol

Email: lrandol@naropa.edu

Lindsey Randol   Counseling psychologist, supervisor, and associate professor in the Mindfulness-based Transpersonal Counseling Master's program at Naropa University. She is also visiting faculty at the Royal University of Bhutan. Lindsey's work focuses on individuals, couples, groups, critical psychology, and the relational and affective dimensions of psychotherapy. In addition to her academic work, Lindsey is in private practice in Boulder, Colorado.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a counselor explores the relational complexities of her pregnancy. Because the visual reality of the pregnancy was hidden beneath the Telehealth screen, the author has the opportunity to decide whether or not to disclose her pregnancy to her clients. The author considers the influences of her training in the United Kingdom and her work in the United States on her therapeutic decision-making and the intersection of cultural, personal, and theoretical contexts and meanings. Through clinical case illustrations, the author discusses themes of therapeutic intimacy, the counselor's subjectivity, and the impacts of self-disclosure on the therapeutic relationship.

Training for the Impossible? Induction and Identity Formation Among Trainee Teachers and Psychoanalysts

David Mathew PHD and Neil Hopkins PHD

Neil Hopkins

Neil Hopkins   Senior Lecturer and Advanced Researcher at the University of Bedfordshire in the United Kingdom. He has published two books: Democracy and Citizenship in Adult and Further Education (Springer 2013) and Democratic Socialism and Education: New Perspectives on Policy and Practice (Springer 2019). He was awarded the British Educational Research Journal's “Editors' Choice Award” in 2020. He has recently co-edited the volume, Reflections on Identity: Narratives from Educators (Springer 2023). He has previously been published in Modern Psychoanalysis.

Psychoanalysis and teaching were what Freud called in 1937, “impossible professions.” The authors explore the systems under which teachers and psychoanalysts are trained in England and how trainees in these professions are inducted into their respective cultures. It's argued that trainees are susceptible to a certain professional and personal vulnerability requiring a strong sense of belonging. The authors go on to discuss how processes such as effective mentoring, supervision and peer support are critical to ensuring new entrants are able to complete training relatively unscathed and with a balanced idea of who they are within their respective areas of work.

In response to the article by Mathew and Hopkins, also in this volume, the author discusses the case study of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis which celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2023. Parsing out what is entailed in training to become a psychoanalyst at this particular institute, the author deconstructs the “impossibility” of the profession and the rigorous nature of process-oriented training. The Psychoanalysis of Artificial Intelligence.: Isabel Millar. Palgrave Macmillan, 2021. 235 pp.

Gwendolyn Burton

Gwendolyn Burton

Gwendolyn Burton  

In The Psychoanalysis of Artificial Intelligence, Isabel Millar uses films, online message boards, corporate discourse, and recent philosophical works about Artificial Intelligence (AI) to show us what we're really doing when we design, fetishize, fear, glorify or fantasize about the particular kind of subjectivity that we deem artificially intelligent. Although Millar is not a clinician, her use of Lacanian psychoanalytic theory brings her reader beyond what mere philosophy and media studies are capable of, in order to show how the self-referential work of conjuring AI into existence (if only in fantasies and fiction) reveals fleshly, embodied, human intelligence and subjectivity.

As with most psychoanalytic inquiries worth their salt, The Psychoanalysis of Artificial Intelligence relentlessly pursues the primal scene of its subject. What is discovered there is at turns uncanny, unexpected, sexy, and terrifying, as the process of conjuring and coding new subjectivities into existences evokes a multitude of fantasies about conception and development, and all the acts and desires associated therein. Mercifully, the terrors Millar depicts do not echo the tiresome annihilation predictions that circulate in headlines today, but delightfully reveal what we don't want to face about our own subjectivity. Spoiler alert: for me, it was the vicious sadism evident in commonplace fantasies of instrumentalizing AI as sexual slaves for some kind of perpetual, pervy lifestyle of continual orgasmic pleasure, but for you, it might be something else, like the fact that the other always remains truly unknowable, whether that other is human, alien, AI, undead, creaturely, or otherwise.

Indeed, our use of AI instantiates a kind of master/slave dialectic, whereby the AI slave seems to us to exist as a kind of instrument for producing knowledge about ourselves and our world.

The author studies his own dream of a colleague's death, linking the content of his dream and the actual death of the colleague in his sleep, both of which occurred the same night. Proposing a model of dream construction, the author integrates perception and archetypal imagery. Theories of Jung, Bion, and contemporary consciousness research are employed to illuminate how this dream arose in what the author describes as a non-local, transpersonal, unconscious mind.

This paper presents the author's theoretical approach to the treatment of seriously disturbed patients, an approach that goes beyond many traditional beliefs and practices within psychoanalysis. Working analytically with such patients requires us to move far beyond the work of interpreting unconscious motivations. The author presents a case illustrating the central importance of what she refers to as “at-one-ment” and “withnessing,” both of which presuppose an approach based on the ontological dimension of human experience and not on the epistemological focus of interpretation.

The author conducted a ten-month treatment of an elderly schizophrenic man in a nursing home during COVID-19. The author observes differences in the beginning, middle, and ending phases of the treatment, despite the treatment being short-term. Reflecting on the experience of working in the setting of a nursing home, the author looks at themes of death and dying, loneliness and isolation, and how the healthcare system treats the elderly.
